consensus_summary: All four blind responses identify the ship primarily as the Church — the vessel of salvation (Barque of Peter, Noah's ark typology) carrying believers through the sea of the world toward salvation, grounded in the storm-calming narratives, Luke 5, and 1 Peter 3:20-21. Secondary meanings listed include the individual life-voyage, worldly commerce/pride (ships of Tarshish, Tyre, Babylon), and Jonah's flight.
book_summary: The book identifies the ship as an earthly kingdom, city, state, or governed political body riding on the sea of peoples — rulers as pilots, inhabitants as crew, armies as defenders, wealth as cargo. It pointedly denies the ecclesial reading: Christ needs no constructed vessel, walking on the sea directly, and when He boards a ship it merely comes under its true Head. The ship may be wrecked while its people survive.
consensus_core_identification: Ship = the Church, the corporate vessel of salvation bearing believers safely through the world.
book_core_identification: Ship = an earthly political body (kingdom, city, state) borne on the sea of peoples, explicitly not the body Christ needs or inhabits by nature.
boundary_disagreement: The book retains the cases the consensus treats as secondary (Tyre in Ezek 27 / Isa 23, Babylon's ships in Rev 18, Jonah's vessel, Paul's shipwreck in Acts 27) as central instances, while stripping the Gospel boat scenes of their ecclesial meaning — the boat with the disciples is not the Church but a constructed body that Christ, who walks the sea unaided, merely subordinates. The Acts 27 detail (ship broken, people saved) is reread as the state perishing while its people survive, inverting the consensus picture of the vessel itself being the means of salvation.
material_contradiction: The consensus says the ship IS the Church, the divinely appointed vessel without which believers do not cross the sea of the world. The book says the ship is a human political construction that Christ does not need, expressly distinguishing Christ (who walks on the water directly) from any vessel; accepting the book requires rejecting the Church-as-ship identification, not merely narrowing it. Additionally, consensus makes the ship the instrument of salvation, whereas the book makes the ship the thing broken while people are saved apart from it.
rationale: Although the book's political/commercial reading overlaps with a listed consensus alternative (ships of Tarshish, Tyre, Babylon as worldly commerce and pride), the alternative was framed as commerce/wealth, and more importantly the book does not merely elevate an alternative — it actively denies the primary consensus identification by arguing Christ needs no ship and that boats in the Gospels are not His body. The central referent is replaced (Church → earthly polity), which is core contradiction rather than boundary refinement, even though extensions partially overlap on the Tyre/Babylon/Jonah/Acts cases.
strongest_objection: One could argue REFINED: the book essentially promotes an already-listed consensus alternative (ships as worldly powers/commerce — Ezek 27, Rev 18, Isa 2:16) to primary status, so the category is recognized within the consensus landscape rather than contradicting it. But the book's explicit denial that Christ's boat represents the Church, and its reversal of the ship's soteriological role, goes beyond re-ranking alternatives to rejecting the consensus core.
